body:
Rule. Hold this rule for Backtracking: Choose, explore, and undo, and prune a partial choice that already fails. Say it before you pick a tool from Algorithms.

Why it matters. Interviewers on the Algorithms track listen for whether you can name the idea backtracking and refuse the common wrong pick. The summary is the force: Choose, explore, and undo, and prune a partial choice that already fails. If you cannot restate it, you will drift into product names or trivia.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: a prompt lands that fits Backtracking. You restate the force in one sentence — Choose, explore, and undo, and prune a partial choice that already fails. — then show a tiny walkthrough that would fail if you ignored that force. You label the SAMPLE answer with the cost or the tradeoff, not with a brand name.

When to use. Use Backtracking when the prompt's access pattern or force matches the summary above, when a prior slug in its after-list is already in hand, and when saying the rule changes which next step you take.

When to refuse. Refuse Backtracking when a simpler tool already covers the force, when a prerequisite in after is still missing, or when applying it would invent a mechanism the track never taught. Prefer naming the missing slug over bluffing.
